metadata.title: Capital-Time Ratios for Different Durations
metadata.description: Compare investments made for different lengths of time before dividing a partnership’s profit.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Calculate each partner’s equivalent capital as capital × duration, then reduce those products to obtain the profit/loss ratio. Handle months, years, and mixed but convertible time units; distinguish the investment amount from the capital-time product. Allocate total profit, find one share, or find the total from a share. Verify by rebuilding the weighted products and checking the shares sum to the total. Use solved examples 2, 7, and 11 and objective patterns 9–18, 36, 42–44, and 54–58.

content.text: Capital-Time Ratios for Different Durations: Compare investments made for different lengths of time before dividing a partnership’s profit. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Capital-Time Ratios for Different Durations asks you to decide what determines each person’s share or assigned amount. Compare investments made for different lengths of time before dividing a partnership’s profit. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. For unequal investment periods, compare the capital-time products rather than the deposits alone. Write the partner or user labels and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

For partner i, use Cᵢtᵢ. A common currency or common time unit is required; a common multiplier may be removed after all products are formed. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once the quantities use compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: A invests ₹38,000 for 12 months; B invests ₹55,000 for 7 months. Their weights are 456,000 and 385,000, so the ratio is 456:385. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Write each partner’s amount and months in a table before multiplying. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. The resulting share ratio should match the direction of the capital-time products: a larger product earns the larger share. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: Do not compare capital amounts alone when durations differ, and do not use the date someone joined as their duration. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. If a total profit is given, divide it according to the reduced weighted ratio; if only a ratio is asked, stop before inventing a total. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for capital-time ratios for different durations without relying on a memorized answer pattern.
